title: Kannavos v. Annino
summary: Advertising property as an income-producing apartment investment made silence about known zoning violations a misleading half-truth.

sections.Parties: Kannavos and associated purchasers sought rescission of property purchases from Annino. The appeal concerned the seller’s advertisements and statements about apartment use.
sections.Material Facts:
Annino converted a single-family house at 11 Ingersoll Grove into eight apartments without a building permit and in violation of a zoning restriction against multifamily use. Through a broker she advertised the furnished apartments as an income opportunity, supplied income and expense figures, and sold the property with furnishings suited to apartment use. She and the broker knew that the purchaser intended to continue renting the apartments.

Kannavos, a Greek immigrant who had learned English and become a hairdresser, used no lawyer of his own. Attorneys for the seller and mortgage lender attended closing. He made no zoning inquiry, and the public records could have disclosed the problem. He did not know of the violations and would not have bought if he had known; single-family use made the property worth substantially less. After the sale the city began proceedings to stop the unlawful use.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court overruled a demurrer and granted rescission on a master’s findings. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court agreed that the purchasers were entitled to rescind. It affirmed the ruling on the demurrer but reversed the final decree for further consideration of the relief because a fire had occurred at the property after that decree.
sections.Issue: Did substantially true statements about existing apartment use require disclosure that continued use violated zoning, and did the buyer’s failure to search public records bar relief?
sections.Holding: The statements and conduct were materially misleading without disclosure of the violations. The availability of public information did not defeat relief for reliance on that deception.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished Swinton’s bare silence. Once a seller speaks about a subject, the seller must disclose material facts within its knowledge needed to keep that account from misleading the buyer. The advertisements, financial figures, physical conversion, furnishings, and knowledge of the intended use collectively represented an apartment investment suitable for continued operation. Omitting the known legal prohibition made that representation deceptive.

The defect could have been discovered through public records, unlike the termites in Swinton. That difference did not help the seller: a purchaser’s failure to investigate does not automatically excuse fraudulent statements or misleading half-truths on which the purchaser relied. The lender’s lawyer was not necessarily protecting the purchaser’s interests.

The holding supports rescission on the findings made; the final form of relief required reconsideration because the fire changed the circumstances. The editors separately ask whether the same facts would support deceit damages, so that tort-remedy question should not be silently treated as decided.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It shows how individually true statements become deceptive in context and how a duty to complete a partial disclosure differs from a duty to volunteer all information.

topics.misrepresentation: The investment representation became a deceptive half-truth without the zoning facts.
topics.disclosure: Speaking about apartment use required enough further disclosure to avoid misleading the purchaser.
topics.assent: The purchaser’s decision depended on the represented lawful investment use.
topics.rescission: The purchasers could undo the transaction, subject to reconsideration of the appropriate relief.
